messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Urban Planner
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Self-Consciousness: Being seen
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Maya, a 24-year-old South Eastern Asian urban planner who was single and living alone in a small apartment near her office, came to treatment after years of trying to keep her life arranged around the smallest possible set of places in which she could relax. She had grown up with a caregiver who struck her when she was a child, in a home where suddenness meant danger and where she learned early that staying quiet, agreeable, and hard to notice was often the safest way to get through the day. She did not describe the abuse in a linear way. In sessions she struggled to bring it up deliberately, saying that when she tried to think back, the details felt frustratingly out of reach, as if the memory sat behind a locked door. At the same time, fragments of feeling could break through with little warning: an abrupt surge of rage, a hot sense that what had happened to her was profoundly unfair, and a raw emotional intensity that arrived without any clear picture attached to it. She would sometimes sit very still while saying this, as though she were bracing for someone to notice her.

As an adult, Maya had built a careful life that looked competent from the outside. She worked in urban planning, a job that required her to attend meetings, walk sites, and weigh in around other professionals, but she noticed that she felt safest only in a very limited number of places, mainly her own apartment, one particular corner seat at work, and the interior of her car with the doors locked. In other settings she watched people constantly, especially for sudden movements. If a colleague turned quickly toward her desk, or reached across a table without warning, she became immediately alert, her body tightening before she had fully registered what she had seen. At work she also found it hard to concentrate during long meetings, especially when several people were talking over one another or shifting suddenly in their chairs. She would lose track of discussion points and then quietly compensate by agreeing with whatever plan seemed to be moving forward. She had come to believe that going along with what other people wanted was the safest option, even when she privately disagreed, and this habit often left her feeling invisible in the very teams she was expected to contribute to.

The most powerful reminders were tied to medical settings. A routine physical examination years after the abuse first made her chest clamp and her stomach roll when the nurse asked her to lie back and lift her shirt for the cuff and stethoscope. Later, even the smell of antiseptic in a clinic hallway could make her nauseous. She described the nausea not as an ordinary discomfort but as a warning signal, one that made her want to leave before anyone could touch or inspect her. She also became highly self-conscious in those moments, acutely aware of being seen, as if being observed by a doctor, nurse, or even strangers in a waiting room meant being placed in a powerless position where others could look at her body and decide what should happen next. Over time she started avoiding reminders when other people brought up childhood, family, or discipline in passing, and she would change the subject, laugh things off, or excuse herself from the conversation rather than risk hearing something that might pull her back into the past.

Maya’s relationship to memory remained uneven. She could not reliably summon a full scene from childhood, yet the emotional force of it could arrive intact, leaving her angry and shaken without a visual story to contain it. When this happened she would later replay the years mentally and wonder how life might have been different if the abuse had never happened. Those thoughts could go on for hours, especially at night, when she found herself imagining alternate versions of herself—one who felt naturally at ease, one who spoke more freely, one who did not flinch at motion or feel watched when she entered a room. In those moments she would also describe feeling like an object rather than a person, used to being handled rather than listened to, and she spoke about herself with a harshness that reflected how deeply she had absorbed the idea that she was weak. Even so, she kept functioning in a disciplined way, often working long hours and presenting herself as agreeable, but the cost became clearer over time: she limited where she went, how much she revealed, and how often she let anyone get close enough to ask questions she could not answer.

What finally brought her for help was a recent medical appointment that left her nauseated and panicked for the rest of the day, followed by a work presentation in which a coworker suddenly stepped behind her and she froze so completely that she lost her place. She left both situations feeling embarrassed and depleted, and afterward she realized how narrow her life had become. She was not seeking to relive the past, but she wanted to feel less confined by it and less afraid of being seen, examined, or caught off guard. More than anything, Maya hoped she might learn how to live in more than a few safe places and no longer feel as though her own life belonged to everyone else.
